analysis.one_liner: Lets federal health officials impose a nationwide eviction ban during disease outbreaks.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have written a nationwide eviction ban back into law after the Supreme Court struck the CDC's order down, was referred to a Senate committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Public Health Service Act to make clear that the Secretary of Health and Human Services can order a moratorium on residential evictions to slow the spread of disease. It would also have immediately required a national eviction moratorium covering all eviction filings, hearings, and judgments, staying in place for at least 60 days after the COVID-19 public health emergency ends. It was a response to the Supreme Court's August 2021 decision blocking the CDC's eviction ban, which the Court ruled exceeded the agency's existing legal authority.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters who could not pay rent during the pandemic would have been protected from eviction filings, hearings, and lockouts automatically, with no application required. Households at risk of homelessness, and community health overall, would have gained from fewer evictions spreading disease. Landlords would still have been owed the rent, but could not remove tenants in the meantime.

how_it_helps.text: It would have required the HHS Secretary to impose a nationwide residential eviction moratorium to reduce the spread of COVID-19, applying automatically to all eviction filings, hearings, judgments, and lockouts without requiring tenants to apply.

It would have rewritten the Public Health Service Act to state explicitly that HHS may use eviction moratoria, closing the legal gap the Supreme Court identified when it blocked enforcement of the CDC's most recent ban on August 26, 2021.

The moratorium would have stayed in effect for at least 60 days after the end of the COVID-19 public health emergency, so renters would not face a wave of evictions the moment the emergency was declared over.

analysis.who_pays: Landlords, especially small landlords who depend on rent income, would have borne the cost of housing tenants who did not pay during the moratorium, while rent debts would still accumulate. The bill contained no compensation mechanism for property owners.

drawbacks.text: Landlords would have been required to keep housing nonpaying tenants indefinitely, with rent arrears piling up and no compensation in the bill; small landlords carrying mortgages could face foreclosure pressure of their own.

After the Supreme Court held that the CDC's ban exceeded the agency's statutory and constitutional authority, opponents argued an eviction moratorium is a housing policy that Congress, not a health agency, should impose through a law that also compensates landlords.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For renters at risk of losing their homes during a pandemic, the protection would have been substantial and immediate. The cost falls on landlords, who receive nothing for housing nonpaying tenants under this bill; that cost is real, hardest on small landlords, and the bill offers them no relief, which is the strongest honest objection to it.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate health committee the day it was introduced and sat there, with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action, until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on September 21, 2021, joined by five other senators, weeks after the Supreme Court blocked enforcement of the CDC's eviction moratorium on August 26, 2021.
The same day it was introduced, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
No further action was ever taken; the committee never reported the bill, and the full Senate and House never voted on it before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and property owners are better off because the nationwide eviction ban never took effect, since they kept the power to evict nonpaying tenants. Renters at risk of eviction got nothing.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to give HHS clear authority to impose eviction moratoria and require one for COVID-19.

against.name: Sen. Patty Murray
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Her committee received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action on it; it never received a hearing or a vote.

against.name: Landlord and apartment industry groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed pandemic eviction bans in Congress and in court and backed the legal challenges that led the Supreme Court to block the CDC's order.

sides.party_line_note: Only six senators, all Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats, ever put their names on the bill; it never reached a vote, so no one else's position was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have barred them from filing, litigating, or executing evictions nationwide during the emergency, while rent debts still accrued and with no compensation. Their interest in regaining eviction power ran directly against renters' interest in keeping their homes.
